title: 12 days, 174 merged PRs: how far can you push AI as the developer and artist of a real game? (WikiDeck, free beta)
author: Old_Discipline_5056
selftext:
Hi r/aigamedev,

I'm a developer and project manager by trade, with several years of experience. I ran an experiment: **keep the project manager role, and let AI be the developer and the artist.** I'm now looking for **beta testers** to see whether the result holds up with real players.

**The game:** [**WikiDeck**](https://wikideck.fr/), a free collectible card game where every card is a real Wikipedia article. A subject's rarity comes from how notable it really is (number of Wikipedia languages, page views). You open boosters, complete themed sets, trade with friends and bid at auction. About 4,800 cards in 45 sets, in English and French, on mobile and desktop.

**What I'd like testers to do:**

* play normally for a few days: boosters, collection, trades, auctions;
* try to break things: weird inputs, many tabs, fast clicks;
* tell me what's confusing, boring, or unfair in the economy.

Bugs can be reported in the game (Help & support page) or in the comments here. I read everything.

**It's free.** There's an in-game currency (Wikis), but **you can't buy it during the beta**, which runs until the end of 2026.

**How it was built (started on October 3):**

* **Me:** product vision, specs, priorities, validating every mockup, testing, and the **architecture**. I designed it to scale from day one: a stateless API running as several instances behind a load balancer, shared state in Redis, background jobs in a Postgres queue, critical rules enforced by the database itself. The AI would not have planned for this on its own: left alone, it builds something that works for one server and breaks at the second.
* **AI as developer:** code, database migrations, tests, deployment config, performance passes, load tests and **security testing** of the code.
* **AI as artist:** card frames and effects, booster packs, icons, interface and mockups, always validated by me on mobile and desktop before any code. The card photos are **not** AI: they are real, freely licensed Wikimedia Commons images.
* **So far:** 292 commits, 174 merged pull requests, \~160k lines of code and \~21k lines of tests.

**What I learned:** productivity is real, but only with structure (specs, small PRs, tests) and a human making the decisions. AI is great at volume and weak at judgment: architecture and content review need a human. This post was written with AI help too, since English isn't my first language.

If you'd like to test it, sign up and say hi in the comments. And if you build games with AI too, I'd love to compare how you organise your projects.

replies.author: Old_Discipline_5056
replies.body: TL;DR: A 12-day case study on human–AI co-development (174 merged PRs, ~160k LOC) testing a strict split where the human acts solely as System Architect and PM, while AI handles all coding and art. The key finding: AI scales output dramatically, but fails at architectural judgment—requiring human-enforced constraints to build scalable, secure distributed systems. Tested on WikiDeck (a free Wikipedia-based CCG), now recruiting beta testers to stress-test system integrity and game economy.

comments.author: madsciencestache
comments.body:
I have a layered orchestration system that alleviates much, but not all of the architecture problem. Runs sprints, leaves human inspectable artifacts. High level docs communicate intent. You can work with AI to create a product plan and then execute the next 4 or 5 slices all at once.

├── project-template

│ ├── [AGENTS.md](http://AGENTS.md)

│ ├── PRODUCT\_PLAN.md

│ ├── specs

│ │ └── 000---example-sprint

│ │ ├── 1\_spec.md

│ │ ├── 2\_spec-review.md 

│ │ ├── 3\_plan.md 

│ │ ├── 4\_plan-review.md 

│ │ ├── 5\_tasks.md 

│ │ ├── 6\_tasks-review.md 

│ │ ├── 7\_test-review.md 

│ │ └── 8\_product-review.md 

│ ├── TECH\_STACK.md 

│ └── WHAT\_AND\_WHY.md

The WHAT\_AND\_WHY.md document is key. If that AI doesn't understand the end goal, it will make it it's business to misunderstand requests! Like a cursed genie.

replies.author: Old_Discipline_5056
replies.body:
Love the "cursed genie" line, that's exactly it. My setup is close but less formal: a CLAUDE.md with the stack and conventions, a SPEC.md for the product, and a DECISIONS.md that logs every change of direction and overrides the spec. That last one is my "what and why": without it, every new session re-opens questions I'd already settled. Each feature gets a mockup that I approve before any code, then small PRs.

Your review steps between each stage are what I'm missing. Running 4 or 5 slices at once, do the reviews catch conflicts between the slices, or do you still merge them one by one?

replies.author: madsciencestache
replies.body:
The previous sprints also serve as context, so the model has a really good idea of what happened before. And the PRODUCT\_PLAN.md has the agreed on sprints. I most ask the AI to propose sprints and then lightly edit if at all before it updates the plan.

Prompt pack is free on my Discord: [https://discord.gg/NRaEvgtPW](https://discord.gg/NRaEvgtPW) and I go over how I use it here: [https://youtu.be/L6Ka3FUe\_B8](https://youtu.be/L6Ka3FUe_B8) (All free, this isn't commercial promotion, but I am trying to build a community/pass on my 30 years of experience.)
